reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Insidious onset means diagnosis is often delayed by years; comparing old photographs can reveal the gradual coarsening of features
Characteristic findings include enlarging hands and feet, coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, and interdental spacing
Soft-tissue overgrowth commonly causes carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia, excessive sweating, and obstructive sleep apnoea
Systemic complications include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and an increased risk of colonic polyps
Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a random GH level is not reliable; IGF-1 is the preferred screening test as it reflects integrated secretion
Biochemical confirmation rests on failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose load
Most cases arise from a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, so pituitary MRI and assessment of other pituitary axes and visual fields are essential
Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the usual first-line treatment, with medical therapy or radiotherapy for residual disease
reference.pathophysiology: Acromegaly is caused by chronic excess of growth hormone, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, and rarely from ectopic GH or GHRH secretion. Excess GH stimulates hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediates most of the peripheral growth effects on bone, cartilage, and soft tissue. When GH excess occurs before epiphyseal fusion it produces gigantism; after fusion it produces the acral and soft-tissue overgrowth of acromegaly. The expanding pituitary mass may also compress the optic chiasm and impair other pituitary hormone axes, while GH's counter-regulatory metabolic effects promote insulin resistance and cardiovascular disease.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional large body habitus or familial coarse features
Pachydermoperiostosis and other causes of acral enlargement
Hypothyroidism causing coarse features and soft-tissue changes
Other pituitary masses causing mass effect without GH excess
Ectopic GHRH or GH secretion from a neuroendocrine tumour
additionalInvestigations: Serum IGF-1 interpreted against age-matched reference ranges as the initial screen
Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement to confirm non-suppression
Pituitary MRI to define adenoma size and relation to the optic chiasm
Formal visual field assessment when a macroadenoma abuts the chiasm
Evaluation of remaining anterior pituitary axes for co-secretion or hypopituitarism
Screening for complications including echocardiography, sleep study, and colonoscopy
redFlags: Visual field loss or new headache suggesting chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma
Features of pituitary apoplexy such as sudden severe headache with ophthalmoplegia
Signs of heart failure from acromegalic cardiomyopathy
Coexisting hypopituitarism, particularly unrecognised adrenal insufficiency
reference.prognosis: Biochemical control that normalises IGF-1 and GH restores life expectancy toward normal and improves soft-tissue and metabolic features, whereas persistent disease increases cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic mortality and the risk of colonic neoplasia.
pitfalls: Relying on a single random GH level, which is uninterpretable given pulsatile secretion
Attributing carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnoea, or new diabetes to common causes without considering acromegaly
Missing coexisting hypopituitarism when focusing on GH excess
Overlooking the need for long-term surveillance for cardiovascular disease and colonic polyps
